text.p: Baseball labour peace became official Friday when representatives of Major League Baseball and the Players Association signed the new collective bargaining agreement.

Donald Fehr, executive director of of the Players Association, and Randy Levine, chief labour negotiator for Major League Baseball, signed the new basic agreement, concluding the often acrimonious labour negotiations that began in 1992.
"This is a great day for baseball," said Levine of the agreement that assures labour peace through the year 2000 with a union option for the 2001 season.
"For the next five years we can concentrate on the game on the field without the distraction of negotiations in the conference room."
Baseball's governing Executive Council Thursday approved the deal that was ratified by the owners November 26. The union approved the deal December 5.
"This marks the beginning of a true renaissance and golden era for the game," said acting commissioner Bud Selig.

The previous labour agreement expired December 31, 1993 and the bitter negotiations that followed led to the players' strike in 1994 that forced cancellation of the second half of the season and the 1994 World Series.
"These have been most ardous negotiations, but players are pleased to have finally concluded a new agreement with the clubs," Fehr said.

The agreement contains a luxury tax and restores the service time lost by players during strike. The deal also calls for revenue sharing to help small-market clubs, and for interleague play, which begins this season.
